overview: The Beothuk were an Indigenous people of Newfoundland whose food, travel and settlement connected the island’s coasts with its interior. Archaeologists trace their history through the Little Passage complex and later sites containing European materials. Houses, tools, food remains and Shanawdithit’s drawings preserve evidence of skills and choices that written colonial accounts often overlooked.

periods.title: The Little Passage archaeological tradition
periods.summary: Stone-tool assemblages associated with the ancestors of the historically recorded Beothuk occur around Newfoundland. The archaeological name describes material evidence, not a separate kingdom or a precise date of ethnic origin.

periods.title: A coastal community at Boyd’s Cove
periods.summary: House pits, animal remains and reworked European metal document a settlement whose occupation is dated approximately 1650 to 1720. Its residents combined local foods with new raw materials.

periods.title: An expedition encounters houses but no residents
periods.summary: John Cartwright traveled up the Exploits River on a mission ordered by Governor Hugh Palliser. He recorded numerous dwellings but did not meet their inhabitants.

periods.title: Shanawdithit records knowledge and experience
periods.summary: In St. John’s, Shanawdithit shared vocabulary and drawings with William Cormack. She died of tuberculosis on 6 June 1829; later accounts raise questions about other survivors.

sections.title: Homes and food in the archaeological record

items.text: At Boyd’s Cove, discarded shellfish helped neutralize acidic soil, preserving tiny fish bones that usually disappear at Newfoundland sites. Smelt bones and remains of seals, caribou, birds and other animals reveal a varied diet. This preservation accident matters: what an excavation recovers depends partly on soil conditions, not only on what people once ate.

Excavators identified eleven house pits at Boyd’s Cove. Most were roughly round or many-sided, while two were oval. Depressions, bark-covered frameworks and earth around the edges offered substantial shelter. Refuse deposited in abandoned pits records later use of those spaces; it should not all be treated as objects left exactly where residents used them.

Seasonal movement allowed people to obtain foods that appeared at different times and places. Coastal marine animals, inland caribou, fish and berries required different knowledge and equipment. A community’s territory therefore included routes and temporary camps as well as larger settlements; one village cannot stand for every household’s annual movements.

Drying and sometimes smoking made salmon and other foods keep longer. Accounts also describe cooking in birchbark containers by adding heated stones to water. These methods joined knowledge of heat, materials and storage with the work of feeding a household. The surviving descriptions do not establish that every meal or every community used identical methods.

Little Passage arrowheads and small hide scrapers from Inspector Island show skilled working of chert. At other sites, such stone tools occur below later deposits containing reworked iron. This sequence is one reason archaeologists connect the Little Passage tradition with the historical Beothuk, rather than interpreting European metal as evidence of an entirely new population.

Nails recovered from seasonally abandoned European fishing stations became projectile points and hide-working tools; fishhooks could become awls. Wrought iron could be reshaped without a forge and bent back when damaged. This was selective adaptation of a useful material to local needs, not the invention of iron or simple dependence on finished European products.

An oval house at Boyd’s Cove contained a long central hearth with finely broken, burnt bone. Researchers compare it with Innu feasting practices in which processed caribou bones had nutritional and spiritual importance. The hearth and bone are excavated evidence; the precise ceremony is an interpretation by comparison, not a witnessed Beothuk ritual.

Campsites and burials are known from many of Newfoundland’s bays, while house depressions also survive beside the Exploits River and the lake historically called Red Indian Lake. This distribution records occupation across different times. It does not establish that one centralized government controlled the entire island at every date shown on the map.

A larger camp could serve as a base while smaller parties used other places for particular resources. Pastore’s reconstruction of Boyd’s Cove contrasts nearby summer foods with harp-seal hunting farther out toward islands and headlands. Such patterns help explain why access to coast and interior both mattered as European settlement increasingly restricted movement.

Shanawdithit’s drawings depict tools, foods, dwellings and encounters with settlers. They preserve knowledge offered by a Beothuk observer, alongside archaeological evidence and outside descriptions. Her work was produced under painful conditions after severe losses in her family and community; it is testimony with a particular history, not an anonymous illustration of a timeless culture.

ending.text: Colonial encroachment, violence, reduced access to food and disease devastated Beothuk communities. Shanawdithit’s death in 1829 is often used to mark their disappearance as a distinct recorded society. Accounts of possible survivors and descendants complicate a claim that every Beothuk person died then. The map’s earlier endpoints are not extinction dates.
